## Problem 1

```{r}
# Birthday function from class
birthday_repeated = function(n_room){
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_room, replace = TRUE)
  
  repeated_birthdays = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_room
  
  return(repeated_birthdays)
}
```

```{r}
birthday_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    number_of_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(number_of_people, birthday_repeated)
  )

birthday_prob_df =
  birthday_results_df |>
  group_by(number_of_people) |>
  summarize(
    prob_of_repeat = mean(repeated)
  )

birthday_prob_df
```

Plot
```{r}
birthday_prob_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = number_of_people, y = prob_of_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Sharing a Birthday by Group Size",
    x = "Number of People in the Room",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The probability of sharing a birthday increases as the number of people in the room increases. With around 23 people, the probability exceeds 50%, and it reaches approximately 97% with 50 people. The increase is nonlinear and gradually levels off as the probability approaches 1.

## Problem 2
```{r}
trial_files = tibble(
  file_name = list.files(
    path = "data",
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    full.names = TRUE,
    recursive = TRUE
  )
)

trial_df = trial_files |>
  mutate(
    subject = str_remove(basename(file_name), "\\.csv$"),
    arm = case_when(
      str_detect(subject, "^con_") ~ "Control",
      str_detect(subject, "^exp_") ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_remove(subject, "^(con|exp)_"),
    measurements = purrr::map(
      file_name,
      ~read_csv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, arm, measurements) |>
  unnest(cols = measurements) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.integer(week)) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

head(trial_df)
```

```{r}
trial_df |>
  count(arm)

trial_df |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarize(
    mean_observation = mean(observation),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
Spaghetti plot
```{r}
trial_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Observations by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observed Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
The spaghetti plot shows different trends between the control and experimental groups over the eight weeks. The control group remains relatively stable, with some fluctuations among individual participants. Its mean observation decreases slightly from 0.92 in week 1 to 0.74 in week 8. In contrast, the experimental group shows a clear increasing trend, with the mean observation rising from 1.14 to 5.12. Although there is some variation between participants, the experimental group generally has higher observed values over time, especially in the later weeks.

## Problem 3

Function
```{r}
set.seed(2026)

sim_ttest = function(mu, n_obs = 30, sigma = 5) {

  sim_df =
    tibble(
      x = rnorm(n = n_obs, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    )

  ttest_result =
    t.test(sim_df$x, mu = 0)

  return_df =
    broom::tidy(ttest_result) |>
    select(estimate, p.value) |>
    rename(
      mu_hat = estimate,
      p_value = p.value
    )

  return(return_df)
}
```

Simulations
```{r}
set.seed(1236)

sim_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(mu, sim_ttest)
  ) |>
  unnest(results)

sim_summary_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(p_value < 0.05),
    mean_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat),
    mean_mu_hat_rejected = mean(mu_hat[p_value < 0.05])
  )

sim_summary_df
```

Plots
```{r}
sim_summary_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Power"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Statistical power increases as the true mean increases. When $\mu$ = 0, the rejection rate is approximately 5.36%, while power increases to 56.06% at $\mu$ = 2 and reaches 100% at $\mu$ = 5. This suggests that larger effect sizes make it easier to reject the null hypothesis.

```{r}
sim_summary_df |>
  select(mu, mean_mu_hat, mean_mu_hat_rejected) |>
  pivot_longer(
    mean_mu_hat:mean_mu_hat_rejected,
    names_to = "estimate_type",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    estimate_type = recode(
      estimate_type,
      mean_mu_hat = "All Samples",
      mean_mu_hat_rejected = "Rejected Samples Only"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = average_estimate, color = estimate_type)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean",
    color = "Sample Group"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The average estimated mean across all samples is approximately equal to the true mean. However, among samples where the null hypothesis is rejected, the average estimate tends to be larger than the true mean, especially for smaller positive effect sizes. For example, when $\mu$ = 1, the average estimate among rejected samples is 2.26. This occurs because samples with more extreme estimates are more likely to produce significant results. As power increases, the difference becomes smaller, and the average estimate approaches the true mean.
